title: Talking about the future
tagline: The future isn't one tense — it's a choice between will, going to and the present continuous.
why: Will is for a decision you make right now or a guess; going to is for a plan already in your head; the present continuous is for something in your diary with a time and a place. Get the choice right and Speaking Part 2 (planning something with a partner) and Writing Part 6 (arranging to meet a friend) both sound natural, not like a grammar exercise.

hook.text: Miss Vega tells the class: "We're going to visit Arequipa next month." "I'll bring my camera!" says Mateo. "We're meeting at the airport at six," adds Miss Vega. "Six? I think I'll be late!" laughs Nadia.
hook.ask: Three different future forms are hiding here — a plan, a fixed arrangement, and a decision made right now. Can you match each one to its job?

watch_out.wrong: I think it will to rain.
watch_out.why: Will is followed straight by the base verb — no to.

watch_out.wrong: We go to visit Arequipa next month.
watch_out.right: We're going to visit Arequipa next month.
watch_out.why: Going to needs am/is/are before it — it can't stand alone.
Shall is followed straight by the base verb — no to, just like will.
A fixed arrangement with a time uses the present continuous, not the present simple.

watch_out.wrong: Look at those clouds — it will rain.
watch_out.right: Look at those clouds — it's going to rain!
watch_out.why: When you can see the evidence right now, use going to, not will.

l1.why: The Spanish 'voy a' becomes am/is/are + going to in English — not just go to.

l1.right: I think it's going to rain.
l1.why: When you can see the evidence now (dark clouds), English prefers going to over will.
A spontaneous offer uses Shall I…? or will, not just the base verb as a question.

l1.wrong: We see each other at six.
l1.why: A fixed plan with a time uses the present continuous in English, not the present simple.

remember.trick: Decide now? WILL. Plan already made? GOING TO.
remember.tip: If you already had the idea before you started speaking, it's going to. If the idea comes to you as you speak, it's will.

can_do: I can use will for decisions I make right now, offers and predictions.
I can use going to for plans I've already made and things I can see coming.
I can use the present continuous for fixed arrangements, and Shall I/we…? for offers and suggestions.
summary: Will + base verb: a decision made right now, an offer, or a prediction (I think it will rain).
Going to: a plan you already had, or something you can see coming right now (look at those clouds!).
Present continuous + a time: a fixed arrangement, already in your diary (we're meeting at six).
Shall I/we…? offers help or makes a suggestion for both of you.
Will and shall go straight to the base verb — no to. Going to and the present continuous both need am/is/are.
